And somewhere high above the city, the first sunlight hits the glass towers.

68.script: FOOD FROM EVERYWHERE If you want to understand Dubai's population, don't look at the skyline. Look at the food. Walk through the city and you can find Emirati dishes, Indian food, Pakistani food, Lebanese food, Filipino food, Chinese food, Turkish food, African cuisines, European restaurants, fast food, street food, luxury dining, and almost everything between them. Dubai has become a giant meeting point for food cultures. A person can eat breakfast from one part of the world, lunch from another, and dinner from somewhere completely different.

87.script: And a strong connection to heritage. The modern skyline does not erase the older identity of the region. You can see traditional dress inside the same city where people wear business suits and tourist clothing. You can find mosques between skyscrapers. You can drink Arabic coffee in a city famous for international luxury. This is another Dubai contradiction. Modernization did not completely replace tradition. It exists alongside it.

121.script: But perhaps the strangest thing about Dubai is not what it has built. It is what it has convinced people is possible. That a city can rise from the desert. That a coastline can be reshaped. That people from almost every corner of the planet can live side by side. And that an environment once considered too harsh for a giant modern city could become the foundation of one. The desert is still there.
